sample_size.excerpt: A total of 34,637 Iowan women initially free of cancer completed a mailed questionnaire in 1986. Kidney cancer incidence was identified over 15 years of follow-up (n = 124) through linkage to a statewide cancer registry.

effect_size.excerpt: The few women who used copper supplements had a 6.52-fold increase in risk of kidney cancer (95% CI = 1.95-21.8). Compared to never users, women who were former users of estrogen had an increased risk of kidney cancer (RR = 1.62; 95% CI = 1.11-2.36), but current users of estrogen were not at a higher risk.

studies.Population: Chinese adults aged 45–74 years residing in Singapore
studies.Smoking Status: Never, former, and current smokers adjusted for in the fully adjusted model
studies.Reference: Dietary Intakes of Trace Elements and the Risk of Kidney Cancer: The Singapore Chinese Health Study.
studies.Authors: Wang Y, Jafar TH, Jin A, Yuan JM, Koh WP
studies.Timing: Dietary intake assessed at baseline in 1993–1998; incident kidney cancer followed through 31 December 2016
studies.comparison_type: Highest versus lowest quartile of dietary copper intake

sample_size.excerpt: Thus, the final sample size for the current analysis was 61,321 participants.

cases.excerpt: There were 229 incident kidney cancer cases after median follow-up of 20.1 years.

effect_size.excerpt: In the fully adjusted model, the HR of kidney cancer risk when comparing the highest versus lowest quartile of dietary zinc was 1.74 (95% CI: 1.02–2.97). Conversely, dietary intakes of copper and manganese were not associated with kidney cancer risk; the corresponding HRs were 1.10 (95% CI: 0.71–1.72; P -trend=0.65) and 1.26 (95% CI: 0.83–1.91; P -trend=0.31), respectively (Model 3; Table 2 ).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Conversely, dietary intakes of copper and manganese were not associated with kidney cancer risk; the corresponding HRs were 1.10 (95% CI: 0.71–1.72; P -trend=0.65) and 1.26 (95% CI: 0.83–1.91; P -trend=0.31), respectively (Model 3; Table 2 ).

p_value.excerpt: Conversely, dietary intakes of copper and manganese were not associated with kidney cancer risk; the corresponding HRs were 1.10 (95% CI: 0.71–1.72; P -trend=0.65) and 1.26 (95% CI: 0.83–1.91; P -trend=0.31), respectively (Model 3; Table 2 ).

comparison.excerpt: For the multivariable analyses, participants were divided in quartiles based on their intake and the lowest quartile intake served as the reference group.

design.excerpt: We used data from the prospective Singapore Chinese Health Study that recruited 63,257 adult Chinese residing in Singapore between 1993 and 1998.

timing.excerpt: Person-year for each participant was counted from the date of baseline interview to the date of death, cancer diagnosis or the end of follow-up (31 December 2016), whichever happened first.

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an effect size of 2.44 (95% CI: 0.43–13.84), indicating no statistically significant association between copper and kidney and renal pelvis cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential positive relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 86.46%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.
